title: Asylum's £5.4B year — Home Office's most expensive ever
hook: In 2023-24 the Home Office spent £5.4 billion on the asylum system — roughly one pound in every four spent by the entire department, and four times what it cost in 2019-20.
lede: Asylum has become the Home Office's largest and fastest-growing budget line. The backlog of undecided cases, hotel accommodation contracts, and the £715m Rwanda preparation all fed a cost curve that quadrupled in five years. Starmer cancelled the Rwanda plan on 6 July 2024, two days after taking office; the £5.4bn steady-state remains.
body_md:
**The £5.4bn.** Home Office accounts for 2023-24 report asylum-system spending of £5.38bn, up from £1.3bn in 2019-20. Of that, roughly £4.3bn went to asylum accommodation (contingency hotels, dispersal housing via the AASC contracts), £500m to asylum support cash payments, £400m to casework and processing, and the balance to returns, detention and enforcement. The PAC called it the department's 'most acute financial pressure'.

**Hotels are the visible cost.** At peak in late 2023, 56,000 asylum seekers were housed in 400+ hotels across the UK at an operating cost of roughly £8m per day. The Bibby Stockholm barge (Portland, Dorset, 2023-24) was presented as a cheaper alternative at £3m/year operating; legionella detection closed it in August 2023; it housed roughly 500 at peak and was decommissioned in January 2025. Hotel use has since reduced to around 220 hotels by end 2024 as the backlog fell.

**The backlog.** Initial-decision backlog peaked at 175,000 cases in mid-2023. The Streamlined Asylum Processing programme (the 'legacy backlog clearance') and the deployment of 2,500 additional caseworkers reduced it to around 55,000 undecided initial decisions by end 2024, though a secondary appeals backlog of roughly 30,000 remains. Clearance has speeded returns of refused cases; grant rates rose to around 65% during the accelerated processing (the legacy cohort had disproportionately strong cases).

**The Rwanda chapter.** Priti Patel's April 2022 Migration and Economic Development Partnership committed £140m upfront to Rwanda, with additional payments contingent on arrivals. The scheme was litigated, amended with the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024, scheduled for first-flight deportations in July 2024 — and cancelled on 6 July 2024, two days after Labour won the general election. Total UK outlay during the preparation phase reached £715m, per NAO; not a single person was deported under the MEDP to Rwanda.

**What replaces it.** Labour's approach, set out in the August 2024 Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Bill and subsequent 2025 legislation: fast-track processing, expanded returns agreements (the EU Reset is seeking a replacement for Dublin), a new Border Security Command, the Channel crossings enforcement unit, and renewed third-country return routes — though explicitly not Rwanda-style processing. Small-boat arrivals in 2024 totalled around 36,800; 2025 first-quarter figures ran above that pace.

**The structural problem.** Asylum processing in the UK has a unique double cost: arrivals cannot work while waiting for decisions (mostly), so the state pays for their subsistence for the duration; and decisions took on average 500+ days through 2023. Any country processing faster, granting work rights sooner, or using community accommodation instead of hotels produces a lower per-case cost. Germany and Denmark spend materially less per claim. The £5.4bn is simultaneously a humanitarian and a fiscal problem — the reform agenda has to reduce both curves at once, which is why it has defeated five successive Home Secretaries since 2019.
